anomaly_def.Name: MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly + Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly
anomaly_def.Description:
MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly : Accumulation of obsolete row versions and rollback records outpaces background cleanup, inflating version stores, bloating storage, and slowing visibility checks.
Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly : Mis-tuned engine settings for memory, checkpointing, logging, parallelism, or worker budgets cause resource-usage patterns that do not align with actual hardware capacity or workload demands.

Composite definition: The database concurrently suffers from excessive MVCC version buildup while critical configuration parameters (e.g., autovacuum thresholds, maintenance work memory, checkpoint intervals, log and buffer sizes) are mis-aligned with the update-heavy workload. The twin conditions coexist, so version store growth is unchecked just as the subsystem meant to reclaim it is throttled or mistimed by sub-optimal settings.

Combined anomalous phenomena:  • Rapid expansion of table and index sizes, soaring obsolete-to-live row ratios, and long sequential scans.  • Cleanup workers that appear active yet never reduce bloat because cost limits, memory quotas, or parallel-worker caps are too low.  • Repeated emergency checkpoints or log-file saturation despite under-utilised I/O bandwidth, coinciding with escalating visibility-check CPU time.  • Planner misestimates and query latency spikes intermixed with seemingly unexplained background I/O storms right after every forced checkpoint.  • Monitoring shows both version-store wraparound warnings and configuration-related wait events (e.g., excessive log flush waits while disks are idle).

Causal interaction: Poorly chosen configuration parameters throttle or mis-schedule the very maintenance tasks needed to prune old versions, letting bloat compound. The swelling version store, in turn, inflates redo volume and dirty-page pressure, triggering more frequent checkpoints and log flushes—events whose impact is magnified by the same mis-tuned parameters governing log size, checkpoint cadence, and buffer pools. As each anomaly feeds the other, the database enters a feedback loop: growing MVCC debris raises I/O and memory demand, while configuration limits prevent timely cleanup, accelerating performance degradation and bringing the system closer to transaction-ID exhaustion or out-of-space failures.

entry.official_description: Out of memory; check if mysqld or some other process uses all available memory; if not, you may have to use 'ulimit' to allow mysqld to use more memory or you can add more swap space
entry.cause_analysis: The failure is typically associated with file creation, filesystem access, write durability, log persistence, tablespace management, or storage-capacity boundaries.
entry.solution_guidance: Inspect filesystem capacity and permissions, verify persistence paths, review log and data placement, and check whether storage latency or write failures are affecting the engine.
